messages.subject: Providing model averaged detection estimates for occupancy model
messages.subject_clean: Providing model averaged detection estimates for occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
I am using a two-stepped approach for modeling occupancy.  First, I determine the "best" detection model while keeping the occupancy side of the model as the null model (i.e. ~ air + water + time ~ 1).  In the second step, I am holding the detection side of the model constant as the top model from the first step.  This is followed by model averaging over the 95% confidence set.  My question is this: is there a way to supply model averaged detection parameter estimates to the second step rather than simply using the top detection model?  Can i do this with the "starts" argument?  If so, how do I incorporate the variability of the estimates?

Thanks,
Nick Smeenk

messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked community,

I'm trying to predict insect abundance across a ~500 ha study site based on repeated count surveys at 20 different trap sites. All traps were sampled once weekly 26 times.

My siteCovs are distance to water (water), distance to large animal feeder (feeder), categorical habitat type (hab), and XY location coordinates standardized into one value with a PCOA (geog). I stacked these rasters, extracted their values at the 20 trap sites, standardized the water and feeder values, and converted hab from numeric to factor to get a data frame of siteCovs.

My obsCovs are weekly utilization distribution rasters (UD) representing large animal blood meal host availability and the date of each survey represented as week 1, week 2, and so on to week 26 (surv_per). I stacked the 26 weekly UD rasters, extracted their values at the 20 trap sites, and standardized those values to create a data frame of obsCovs. To include surv_per in my obsCovs, I made an M x J matrix of survey periods like so:

> survey_per <- matrix(rep(1:26, each = 1, times = 20), ncol = 26, nrow = 20, byrow = T) # Make matrix of survey period/site
> survey_per <- as.data.frame(apply(survey_per, MARGIN = c(1,2), FUN = factor)) # Convert numbers to factor, coerce into data frame

My best model is:
> stel_16_p_A

Call:
pcount(formula = ~UD + surv_per ~ feeder + water + hab + geog,
    data = stel_16_p_UMF, K = 2000, mixture = "NB")

Next, I want to produce maps of estimated weekly insect abundance across my study site with my raster stacks. Based on other posts in this group (such as by N. Angeli <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/predict$20raster%7Csort:date/unmarked/QTPK3ujKVEc/j5x4jRYWJwcJ> & M. Spinola <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/unmarked/qdebFD9g_r8/r06gUAnPjD4J>), I started with stacking my site raster stack and one UD raster (say week 1's)  together, but I'm stumped on how to include surv_per in the predict() function since it's not spatial. That's likely why I'm getting the error below?

> stack_all <- stack(site_stack, UDs_2016$week1)
> names(stack_all) <- c("hab", "feeder", "water", "geog", "UD")
> week1_pred <- predict(stel_16_p_A, newdata = stack_all, type = "state")
Error in .local(obj, coefficients, ...) :
  ncol(coefficients) == length(obj@estimates) is not TRUE

Is it possible to include an aspatial covariate in a spatial prediction? I appreciate any insights into my work here.

Please let me know if you need any further information.

Best,
Emily

messages.subject_clean: Aspatial covariate in N-mixture model maps for abundance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Emily,

If I understand correctly, you want to predict abundance in each of your 26 survey periods (weeks). The static N-mixture model (in the way you've employed it) assumes abundance does not change (the closure assumption), but it can be worked to estimate weekly abundance (see below).

Taking a step back, in the current model, you're hypothesizing that detectability (of the static abundance per point) varies with your two obsCovs: UD (blood meal host availability) and surv_per (weeks, as a factor). You hypothesize (static) abundance varies with your siteCov variables. As you currently have it, the only dynamic (weekly by trap) estimate you can generate is a probability of detection (which is sometimes of interest to folks). I don't think that's what you want.

If, however, you suspect abundance does change over your 26 weeks (and you want to estimate this changing abundance across trap sites), you'll need to think about what constitutes a period of closure. If, for example, this period is four weeks, you have a couple (or more) options. The first option is to continue using the static N-mixture model and stack your observations and siteCovs as 20 rows (20 trap sites x 7 4-week periods, rounding up). You'll find examples on other threads. Alternately, you could use the Dail-Madsen dynamic N-mixture model which allows you to model the change between 4-week periods. Defining a period of closure may be your biggest challenge here but it's critical to nail that down.

In terms of your specific error, I suspect it might be levels and/or ordering of factors in your hab covariate (also examples on other threads). However, even if you can get this to work, you'll only have a single, static output.

HTH

Giancarlo

Hi,

taking a quick look at the code and data you sent, here are a few issues I noticed:

-you are using binary data (detected/not detected) for the species data, whereas you are requesting an N-mixture model (i.e., pcount( )) which requires count data. The data type you are using is not appropriate for pcount( ), you should look into occupancy models instead.

-you have quite a lot of explanatory variables on both the abundance and detection parts of the model and the pcount( ) code you sent returns an error (Hessian is singular.  Try using fewer covariates.).

I suggest reconsidering the type of analysis you are using and reading up on the type of data appropriate for these analyses.

Best,

Marc

 if you specify knownOcc for some sites then it changes the likelihood for those sites to include only detection parameters (normally when occupancy status is not known a priori then the likelihood for the data from a given site includes both p and psi parameters). To be honest I can't remember where this is discussed explicitly in the literature.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am running a single-season occupancy analysis using remote camera data via the "occu" function for 3 different species, surveyed at 85 sites for 44 weeks in 3 different treatments. I have treated "species" and "treatment" as factored variables. For reasons beyond my level of understanding, the occupancy coefficients for 1 of my 3 species are very large, with wonky standard error estimates and CIs crossing 0. I am running a candidate set of 29 models, but I see the issue arises for the first time even in a very basic model with detection held constant and no additional co-variates included beyond an interaction term between species and treatment:

m9<-(occu(~1~species*treat,OCC))

Call:
occu(formula = ~1 ~ species * treat, data = OCC)

Occupancy (logit-scale):
                Estimate     SE        z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)        0.746  0.405  1.84270  0.0654
species2           0.355  0.595  0.59559  0.5514
species3          10.145 43.797  0.23163  0.8168
treat2             0.823  0.637  1.29270  0.1961
treat3             1.820  0.838  2.17152  0.0299
species2:treat2   -0.958  0.877 -1.09290  0.2744
species3:treat2   -0.334 70.342 -0.00475  0.9962
species2:treat3   -1.129  1.088 -1.03753  0.2995
species3:treat3   -9.420 43.815 -0.21500  0.8298

Detection (logit-scale):
 Estimate     SE     z   P(>|z|)
   -0.802 0.0246 -32.6 5.47e-233

AIC: 9761.832
Number of sites: 255
optim convergence code: 0
optim iterations: 38
Bootstrap iterations: 0

I do not have this issue with the other 2 species in any of the models, even with the inclusion of site-level and time-varying co-variates. I am having no issues with detection coefficients for any of the species. All of the species have the same number of "NA"s because surveys for all 3 species come from the same sites. The occupancy estimates I get for species 3 in all 3 treatments is very close to 1, and detection rates averaged ~52-58% in all three treatments.

I'm wondering if anyone has any insight as to why I'm getting these results? I have a feeling it may be a simple answer based on the underlying probabilities of occupancy and detection. I am aware of possible issues with extrinsic non-identifiability, but I am not statistically savvy enough to identify if that is the issue, and if it is I am unsure how to proceed. I investigated the raw detection data a bit and did see that I had a relatively equal number of detections and non-detections across all 3 treatments for species 3 (1659=1, 1435=0), so I'm wondering if (since I had a roughly 50% chance of detection and 50% naive occupancy) the model cannot accurately estimate the error for the occupancy coefficients? Perhaps I am way off base here...  I would certainly appreciate any input, and please forgive me if I am asking questions with obvious answers. Thanks in advance for your time.

Sincerely (a struggling graduate student),
Andria Townsend

Dear Andria,
 how many of the 85 sites was species 3 detected at? If the species was detected at all of the sites (or almost all) than the MLEs will behave like you observe here because psi = 1 for that species, I.e, the boundary of the parameter space. In that case then the numerical estimate of the Hessian used to compute the asymptotic SE is invalid.  There's nothing you can do about this -- but its also not a problem because the MLE is merely indicating this pattern (i.e., psi = 1).
regards,
andy

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Previously I developed an unmarkedFrameOccu using covariates and i had no issue as below:

occ <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = dethist,
                             siteCovs = site_covariates,
                             obsCovs = NULL)  # because there are not survey-level covariates

But, today I am using another data set with only detection history with no data for covariates. For this i created the unmarkedFrameOccu object as below:
umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=data1)

then i created the null model as below:
null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf,)
this returned error as "Error: Hessian is singular.  Try providing starting values or using fewer covariates."

then i tried to use the below models using start and se:
null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf, starts=c(1,0))
null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf, se=F)

Using the above two starts and se, the model ran with no error.
They gave same detection estimates but the SE, Z and other values came out as NA. Further the occupancy estimates differed in both estimates.

Then i tried to swap the starts=c(1,0) to starts=c(0,1) and and this gave the same error as this model null <- occu(~1 ~1, umf,)

My questions are:

1. Firstly why does this error arise? Is it due to too little data or too many data? (# of observations). For this data set I had 34 rows and 123 columns
2. why is a starting value needed? And does the sequence of 0, 1 matter ?
3. What is the suggested approach to deal with such issues?

Your support and inputs will be highly appreciated.

Dechen

The principle behind MLE is that the best guess for a parameter value theta is that value of theta for which pr(data|theta) is greatest. In practice, your computer is using some algorithm to iteratively guess at values of theta until it finds those values where pr(data|theta) is greatest. Sometimes, the computer doesn't quite do as well as one would like. For example, it might explore some wildly incorrect part of the possible parameter space and converge upon some local optima (a combination of values for which the likelihood is greater than nearby combinations of parameter values); it might explore some wildly incorrect part of the possible parameter space where all guesses are extremely and nearly equivalently unlikely and ultimately give up and provide some convergence error. These issues can be more likely to occur if the algorithm starts its sequences of guesses in said bad part of the parameter space, and entering arguments for starting values is one way to make sure the algorithm at least starts its guesses with plausible values. Maybe the easiest way to specify starting values is to look at the the estimates from a similar/nested model using the same data.
Re. the sequence and specific values used: for a occu model ~1~1, one value corresponds to p on the logit scale, and one to psi on the logit scale because this is the link function used(I don't remember whether detection or occupancy comes first). The inverse logit of 0 or 1 respectively equals 0.5 or about 0.7, for what it's worth: these might or might not be realistic starting values for what you've got.
The variance covariance matrix and standard errors are derived from the Hessian matrix, which is based on second deriviatives of the likelihood w/ respect to the parameters (if there's a really pronounced maxima w/r/t some parameter, the SE is smaller). If you specify se=FALSE, than the call to occu does not include calculating the Hessian, and so both you avoid any error about it being singular and cannot estimate standard errors
Calculation of the Hessian is more difficult and can fail when the model is very complex (overfit) or if the optimizer ends up on some ridge in the likelihood, hence the error message.
As to what is triggering the error with your data...completely speculating, but perhaps p is very low?

Cheers,

John

I'm really a newbie in R and occupancy modeling, but I think I understand the solution to your problem.
First  you can use the backTransform () to estimate the parameters with covariates but it is used in the following way

backTransform (linearComb (fm62, type = "state", coefficients = c (1,0)))

  1 is your intercept and every 0 is the average of the covariate, there must be as many 0 as the number of covariates in your model, that is, if there are 4 covariates, you have to have four 0 (unless you want to estimate the value when determined covariable is different from your average).

this link could be of help
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/unmarked.pdf

However the predict function has more applicability

If you try to predict your example model, when you create the newdata you have to add the rest of the covariates and the way to do it depends if they are categorical or continuous. You would try in this way since your covariates are continuous

Newdat1 <- data.frame (FELINE = 0, DCENPOB = 0, DFAGUA = 0, DAPROT = seq (min (DAPROT), max (DAPROT)))

predict (fm80, type = 'state', newdata = Newdat1, appendData = TRUE)

Hope this can help you.

In case anyone else ends up here, I tried to fit a different model also with a covariance matrix (from Marc's BPA book, p206) and came up with the same error message "Error in mcmc.list(x) : Different start, end or thin values in each chain".

The issue seems to be the adaptation phase, which seems to end up taking a different number of iterations in the different chains, so when the output is combined the chains don't match in length. I manually set n.adapt= to force the same number of adaptation iterations in each chain. Note the JAGS manual recommends n.adapt=1000 as a minimum, though if you set it to fewer (as I did initially) it will report if it thinks adaptation hasn't been achieved.

Why this should be, and why it might differ on different computers I don't really know, but the fix seems to work for me - I hope it does for you too...

Cheers
Rob

messages.subject: N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?
messages.subject_clean: N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?
messages.body_plain:
Greetings to all,

I have a question regarding the suitability of N-mixture models for our analysis of the relative abundance of prey species in the landscape, and I was hoping for the forum’s candid opinion/comments/suggestions.

Background:

Together with colleagues, we are analysing ungulate count data from road surveys in a large landscape in Africa, with the intent of examining how medium/large herbivores influence lion resource selection.

The data on the prey species was obtained during single-visit surveys of roads, where we counted tracks. From the number of tracks traversing the road, we estimated the number of individuals detected in each spatial replicate (2km road segments). There is no difference in the road substrate – it is all sand, and tracks are typically easy to see. We have ~475 sites (i.e. 64 km2 square grids) with typically three to seven 2-km segments within each cell (spatial survey replicates).

Since we are not interested in specific species’ relative abundance, we have lumped detections of lion prey species in three categories/”species” - small/medium/buffalo. “Downgrading” our data to 0/1 detection – non-detection, we saw that there is clear evidence of heterogeneity in detection probability of prey due to abundance variation among sites (as expected Royle-Nichols models performed much better than MacKenzie models). Also, thankfully, there was no evidence that there is need to consider Hines models of spatial-correlation in detection of prey in the adjacent road segments (i.e. the 2km segments were sufficient large). This analysis was run in Presence stand-alone software because of the need to consider Hines models as well.

Question:

We plan to use N-mixture (pcount) models for our analysis from now on, to make most of the data in hand – i.e. the counts. We understand that we are not interpreting N to mean abundance but a relative abundance across our sites. However, we are concerned by the fact that our ungulate species that we have lumped together in small/medium/large species detection/count histories are – some of them at least – group living animals.

According to the AHME book by Kery et al, “N-mixture models assume independence of detection, meaning individuals are detected independent from each other.” When we are dealing with animals occurring in groups, clearly we have the case where herds are easier to detect than solitary animals.

Remember, what we want from this analysis is to obtain three good models for the relative abundance of small/medium/large “species” of lion prey in the very large landscape, and – using spatial covariates – to generate predictive maps of lion prey availability in the entire landscape (even where we did not survey), so as to feed them as covariates in lion resource selection models.

So, is the group living natural history of our ungulates complicating our analysis to an extent that we should fall back to using Royle-Nichol models (and loose therefore the wealth of the count data that was painstakingly collected)?

Thank you very much for your suggestions. Searching the forum we did not find a similar discussion, and hopefully this question is of value to other people considering similar analysis (as more and more people try to “adapt” N-mixture models to their own research needs).

Thank you in advance.

Christos

messages.body_plain:
Dear Andy,

First of all, thank you for taking the time to reply to the post. Discussing with the people who oversaw the data collection, we have a situation where skilled trackers counted fresh (day-old at most) tracks of ungulates crossing the sandy roads. As I understand it, the assumption violation of concern here is that antelope A that is part of a herd is likely more "visible/detectable" than antelope B that is moving alone and this means that the two antelopes differ in their detection probability.

This difference in detectability would be (as I think about it) more of an issue if we were counting actual observed animals than tracks. Indeed, a herd of impala would attract ones attention and be spotted more often than a solitary impala. However, our trackers were moving along the road and had plenty of time (and tracking skills) to detect both solitary and herd moving animals as their tracks on sand are clear. Would the "herdiness" (grouping) of some tracks really make them more "detectable"? I see how one could make a point that this would not be the case. I am not asking this to try and find a way to wiggle around model assumption violations, but rather to better understand whether tracks can be used in general with N-mixture models. Of course, even if this was the case, we are left with the possibility that some of the tracks are of non-unique animals, as you say - i.e. that we may have double counted tracks of the same animal in the same survey period (here a spatial replication --> survey road segment of 2 km length).

Most importantly however, why would "falling back" to using Royle-Nichols models (occuRN) would be also non advisable here? We would be using binary detect/non-detect data from each segment. How is the group moving nature of the study animals a concern here? Apologies if I am missing the obvious.

Finally, Martin et al. (2011) ("Accounting for non-independent detection when estimating abundance of organisms with a Bayesian framework") which you co-authored, introduces a beta binomial model that introduces a correlation parameter for animals living in a group (manatees in that case). Is that the path that you would recommend we look into when you mentioned above "modifications of the model could accomodate that", or did I misunderstand that?

Thanks again! Always great to learn (even if via many trials and errors).

Christos + team
